title: Iglesia Ni Cristo Extends Humanitarian Assistance to Nepal Following Devastating Floods - AOL.com

full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sep 29, 2026--

The Iglesia Ni Cristo (Church of Christ), under the leadership of Executive Minister Brother Eduardo V. Manalo, has extended humanitarian assistance to Nepal following the devastating floods that caused widespread loss of life and extensive destruction across affected communities.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260929255762/en/

Nepalese government officials and Church representatives: Nepalese government officials receive humanitarian assistance from the Iglesia Ni Cristo as the country continues relief, recovery, and rebuilding efforts following widespread flooding. In photo from left to right: Ramesh KC (Himalaya TV), Rebika Chhetri (Journalist and TV Host), Suraj Vaidya (Honorary Consul General of the Philippines to Nepal), Shyam Kadel (Executive Director, Himalaya TV), Willen Regalado (Supervising Minister, Ecclesiastical District of Thailand), Swarnim Wagle (Minister of Finance, Nepal), Randy Fatallo (Minister of the Gospel), Edwin Estrellado (Asst. Supervising Minister, Ecclesiastical District of Thailand), Caesar Vallejos (President, NET25)

Through the Felix Y. Manalo Foundation, the humanitarian arm of the Iglesia Ni Cristo, a dedicated Church delegation traveled to Nepal to personally convey the Church's solidarity with the Nepalese people and extend financial assistance for ongoing disaster response and recovery efforts.

The Iglesia Ni Cristo and the Felix Y. Manalo Foundation provided US$200,000, equivalent to approximately NPR 30.556 million , which was formally turned over in Kathmandu to Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle for the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund .

The assistance comes as Nepal continues to confront the devastating consequences of severe flooding, including loss of lives, missing persons, displacement, and extensive damage to homes, infrastructure, roads, bridges, agricultural lands, schools, hospitals, and hydropower facilities.

The scale of the destruction has been described as unprecedented. Accounts shared in connection with the disaster response characterized the flood as resembling a tsunami, with floodwaters moving with extraordinary speed through areas where communities depended on rivers and surrounding lands for their homes and livelihoods.

Beyond the immediate human toll, the disaster has inflicted severe economic and physical damage. Thousands of homes were reportedly swept away, while critical infrastructure and agricultural areas suffered extensive destruction. The resulting reconstruction and recovery requirements are expected to be substantial.

Speaking during the assistance turnover, representatives of the Nepalese government expressed appreciation for the Iglesia Ni Cristo's contribution and its gesture of solidarity with the people of Nepal.

The assistance was welcomed as an expression of common humanity , particularly as Nepal undertakes rescue, relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction efforts.

Government representatives also thanked Brother Eduardo V. Manalo for considering Nepal's urgent needs and directing humanitarian assistance to the country, despite the Philippines facing its own disasters and humanitarian challenges.

The Nepalese officials emphasized that the Church's decision to extend assistance was deeply appreciated by the Nepalese people and described the contribution as generous and meaningful to the country's disaster-relief efforts.

For the Iglesia Ni Cristo, the humanitarian mission reflects its continuing commitment to extend compassion and practical assistance to people affected by disasters, regardless of nationality or religious affiliation. Through the Felix Y. Manalo Foundation and its Care for Humanity initiatives, the Church has provided humanitarian assistance in communities affected by natural disasters and other hardships in various parts of the world.

The Nepal mission likewise demonstrated that humanitarian solidarity can transcend borders, bringing people together in times of profound suffering.

“ We are all working to advance the common humanity. ”

The Iglesia Ni Cristo remains committed to standing with communities affected by calamities and to extending assistance, compassion, and hope to those facing the difficult road toward recovery.

“We have had a number of wake-up calls, with the region seeing back-to-back mega-hazards. What is evident is that this is now a slap in the face and time is running out,” he said.

Preliminary scientific assessments indicate that an ice-rock avalanche triggered flood. ICIMOD found that across the Himalayas, glaciers are retreating which is increasing the need for science-based preparedness and long-term investment in resilience.

The latest action points call for redesigning early-warning triggers to account for sudden-onset hazards and improving lead times for communities. They also propose exploring “sacrificial infrastructure” that could absorb the impact of cascading hazards.

Other recommendations include creating an inventory of multi-hazard hotspots using satellite monitoring and impact-based forecasting; shifting trans-boundary cooperation from sharing raw data to providing decision-ready information; and conducting a regional assessment of disaster-response resources and capacities.

description: Nepal approves bill on civil servants’ retirement — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
The Government of Nepal has approved a bill amending the Civil Service Act, paving the way for its submission to parliament. The document provides for the one-time mandatory retirement from civil service of employees who will be 55 years old when the law comes into force or who will have 30 years of service, Kathmandu Post reports.

Pension payments

The bill includes provisions to preserve pension payments for civil servants who will be retired under the new rules. The changes were made following recommendations from the Public Service Commission, which drew attention to legislative guarantees concerning civil servants’ terms of service and social benefits.

According to a ministry official, employees retired solely because they have reached the age of 55 may be credited with up to three additional years of service for pension calculations, up to the current mandatory retirement age of 58. Those with 30 years of service may be credited with up to seven additional years depending on their age. For example, a civil servant with 30 years of service who is 51 may have seven years of service added for pension calculations.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Transitional rule

Current Nepalese legislation sets mandatory retirement for civil servants at the age of 58 and does not include a requirement to retire after a specified number of years of work. The bill defines the age threshold of 55 or 30 years of service as a one-time transitional measure.

For employees who remain in service after this provision is applied, the retirement age limit is planned to be raised to 60. The Public Service Commission has also expressed concerns about differing rules for certain groups of employees and the possible deterioration of service conditions without their consent.

Bills concerning civil service were previously submitted to the House of Representatives in 2017 and 2022, but were not adopted. The current draft is to be sent to parliament after the government decision is formalized.

title: Nepal dispatch: Bhotekoshi disaster tests the limits of climate adaptation - Jurist.org
description: Nepal dispatch: Bhotekoshi disaster tests the limits of climate adaptation  Jurist.org
publisher.title: Jurist.org
full_article:
Voimo Tamang is a third-year law student at National Law College and a JURIST correspondent based in Kathmandu, Nepal.

On September 24, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah addressed the 81st United Nations General Assembly to bring the country’s devastating Bhotekoshi–Trishuli floods to the center of the international climate debate. Describing the disaster as a warning for the world, Shah argued that climate catastrophe is not only a humanitarian crisis but a development emergency, as disasters can destroy roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms, and energy infrastructure, forcing vulnerable countries to borrow in order to rebuild. He called for adequate grant-based support, faster and simpler access to climate finance, and stronger international cooperation on climate resilience.

Shah also proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism involving Nepal, India, and China. The proposed mechanism would facilitate the sharing of satellite data and technical expertise, monitoring of dangerous glacial lakes, stronger early-warning systems, and coordinated cross-border assistance during disasters. His proposal reflects a basic reality of Himalayan climate risks: hazards do not stop at national borders.

The August 26 disaster that prompted the speech began when a massive rock-and-ice avalanche near the Nepal–China border developed into a debris flood and swept downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli corridors. According to the Nepal government’s initial flood briefing , the disaster caused extensive loss of life and damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, and other critical infrastructure. Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other districts were affected.

By September 25, it was reported that 1,453 bodies had been recovered, while 4,718 people remained missing. Police also reported that DNA samples were being collected to identify recovered bodies and that thousands of personnel had been deployed for search, rescue, relief, and related operations. Search and identification operations are continuing, and the figures remain subject to change.

The government’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) estimated approximately NPR408 billion in damage and economic losses and approximately NPR 723.31 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs. Infrastructure accounts for the largest share of the reconstruction requirement, including roads, bridges, and energy infrastructure. A more comprehensive Post Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) is still underway, which is expected to provide a fuller assessment of the disaster’s economic, social, and other losses.

The scale of the response has also required sustained coordination between Nepal’s disaster-management authorities, security agencies, and local governments. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ daily situation updates have documented the continuing search, rescue, and relief operations, in addition to coordinating with neighboring countries and international partners.

After the disaster, the government introduced a “ one-door ” system to collect and distribute relief. Individuals, private companies, donor agencies, and international organizations have channelled cash and in-kind assistance through designated government mechanisms. The system was intended to prevent irregularities and duplication, and to coordinate distribution through government agencies and local authorities.

The disaster also raises a more difficult question about climate change. A September 2026 assessment by World Weather Attribution (WWA) found that the event began with a catastrophic rock-and-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood. The researchers linked the changing Himalayan environment—including warming, glacier loss, and permafrost degradation—to conditions that can increase the instability of mountain landscapes. The study does not suggest that climate change alone caused the collapse. Rather, it points to climate change as one factor interacting with existing geological vulnerabilities.

This distinction matters. Simply calling the disaster a “climate disaster” risks overlooking its geological causes, while treating it as purely geological ignores evidence that a warming Himalaya is changing the conditions in which mountain hazards occur. The WWA assessment found that the disaster exposed adaptation limits, particularly where existing warning and preparedness systems are confronted with rapidly developing, cascading hazards.

Nepal’s climate policy already recognizes the problem of loss and damage. Its 2025 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) identifies the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) and the Santiago Network as important sources of support. It also commits Nepal to improving the documentation of economic and non-economic losses and following a “build back resilient” approach to recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction.

The Bhotekoshi disaster has now put those commitments to a practical test. Nepal had already been approved for approximately US$20 million under the FRLD’s Barbados Implementation Modalities, based on proposals submitted before the August disaster. Separately, Nepal submitted an urgent request to the FRLD Board on August 31 seeking assistance following the Bhotekoshi disaster. The two forms of funding should not be treated as the same: the first relates to previously submitted proposals, while the second was an emergency request made after the disaster.

This gap between policy commitments and emergency access to finance is where the climate-justice question becomes particularly important. International climate frameworks recognise the vulnerability of developing countries, but communities affected by a disaster cannot rebuild with principles alone. They urgently need funding, technology, and institutional support to prevent a temporary disruption from becoming long-term development loss.

Nepal’s experience also shows why climate justice is not only about compensation. It involves who bears the cost, who has access to decision-making, and whether vulnerable communities can participate in decisions about reconstruction and relocation. The government’s response therefore needs to consider not only how quickly damaged infrastructure can be replaced, but where and how it should be rebuilt.

For a country whose mountain terrain creates unavoidable exposure to geological hazards, resilience cannot mean promising that disasters will never happen. It must mean reducing avoidable vulnerability before the next disaster occurs. That includes stronger early-warning systems, better mountain monitoring, cross-border information sharing, climate-resilient infrastructure, and clearer plans for communities living in high-risk areas.

The Bhotekoshi disaster leaves Nepal with two connected challenges. Internationally, it must turn its call for climate justice into accessible finance and regional cooperation. Domestically, it must ensure that reconstruction does not simply recreate the vulnerabilities that existed before August 26.

The next test will be whether Nepal’s UN appeal translates into concrete climate finance, and whether the government’s reconstruction plans can turn the lessons of Bhotekoshi into stronger protection for communities facing an increasingly unstable Himalayan environment.

title: Opinion | If AI automates work, how will Nepal fund the state? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | If AI automates work, how will Nepal fund the state?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s National AI Policy (2025) promises higher productivity, better public services and a workforce ready for the Artificial Intelligence (AI) economy. These are reasonable, even necessary goals for a developing country like ours. But the policy is largely silent on socio-economic questions such as what happens to employment, the tax base and the state’s ability to fund itself when machines begin to replace workers at scale.

In Nepal, unemployment already stands at around 10 percent . Tax revenue accounts for roughly 90 percent of government revenue , while remittances have recently been equivalent to 26 to 33 percent of national GDP. In the near future, if automation significantly shrinks formal wage employment, it could weaken these very pillars of our economy, leading to serious fiscal consequences. For a country that neither builds frontier AI systems nor maintains a strong social safety net, the first policy question should not be how much productivity AI can unlock, but whether it will deepen the fractures already visible in our economy.

For most of modern economic history, labour, growth and state revenue moved together. Workers produced value, consumers spent it, and governments taxed the results. AI disrupts this relationship because capital in the form of AI models, agents and robots can now perform tasks that once required skilled human time, thereby removing labour from the equation. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, this substitution may extend beyond low-skill work into high-skill sectors, precisely the areas Nepal aspires to build its future workforce around.

Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu used the term “ productivity bandwagon ” to explain how technological progress can improve society broadly. But for that to happen, two conditions must be met: (i) Technology must increase workers’ productivity, and (ii) Workers must retain enough bargaining power to claim a share of the resulting gains.

Nepal’s AI policy focuses almost entirely on the first condition and says almost nothing about the second. When labour becomes easier to replace, employers gain greater leverage over wages and working conditions, while a larger share of the gains goes to the owners of the technology. Something similar happened during the Industrial Revolution, when Britain went through a long stretch known as “Engels’ Pause”, during which output and profits rose while worker wages stagnated and their living conditions worsened. A similar imbalance is beginning to appear today: record numbers of applicants per opening, shrinking entry-level roles and widespread layoffs.

Nepal’s exposure to such vulnerabilities is immediate. For instance, the country’s IT and software service exports are estimated at nearly $1 billion annually, which is an important and growing source of foreign earnings, yet the sector is one of the first exposed to AI automation. IT is only one part of a much broader shift, as pressure will eventually move towards other white-collar jobs. And as AI advances alongside robotics and physical automation, it will reach a wider range of jobs that still employ large numbers of Nepalis at home and abroad.

Meanwhile, the infrastructure that powers most advanced AI sits in a handful of wealthy economies, referred to as the “Compute north”. Nepal, like most developing economies, sits in the “Compute south”: a consumer of AI capability rather than a producer. Payments for such AI services flow outward even as the efficiency they enable reduces local labour demand. As a result, Nepal risks bearing the domestic cost of AI-driven displacement while much of the corresponding value is captured abroad.

The policy response should therefore begin with socio-economic and fiscal risks, not only with productivity targets. Three areas of action could help the government improve Nepal’s position.

First, build a real data baseline. The government should publish an annual assessment of how automation is affecting employment and output by sector. Without reliable numbers, every policy-level decision is just guesswork.

Second, protect workers during the transition. Upskilling programmes are necessary but insufficient on their own. Temporary income support, training stipends and active job-matching for those displaced by algorithmic change could reduce the human and political cost of the shift.

Finally, Nepal should explore new revenue sources that track the technology itself. As the traditional income-tax base comes under pressure, it should study mechanisms, already being discussed in several advanced economies, to capture value from AI usage at the point of consumption. Major AI platforms already meter and bill AI tokens (which is the basic unit of data processed by AI models), so the technical capacity to track domestic use exists. A tax on AI tokens consumed in Nepal could retain a share of the economic activity that occurs in Nepali territory.

title: More than 21,500 borrowers blacklisted in Nepal — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: More than 21,500 borrowers blacklisted in Nepal — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, more than 21,500 borrowers were blacklisted during the 2025–2026 financial year for failing to repay microfinance loans. This accounts for about 36% of all borrowers added to such a list during the year, Kathmandu Post reports.

According to the Nepal Credit Information Centre, 170,000 people are currently blacklisted, including 31,797 clients of microfinance institutions. Over the past four years, the number of blacklisted microborrowers has risen from 710 in the 2022–2023 financial year to 3,600 in 2023–2024, 5,800 in 2024–2025, and about 21,600 in 2025–2026.

Reasons for rising debt

Experts link the situation to a decline in economic activity, falling incomes and demand, as well as restrictions imposed by Nepal's central bank on obtaining loans from multiple microfinance institutions. Current rules allow one borrower to take loans from a maximum of two such institutions.

Previously, some small entrepreneurs took out new loans to repay the principal and interest on earlier loans. After problems in the cooperative sector and the introduction of restrictions on multiple lending, this disrupted the cash flow on which small businesses depended.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Former central bank executive director Prakash Kumar Shrestha said that during the period of rapid expansion, microfinance institutions aggressively increased lending to meet targets and did not always properly select borrowers in line with microfinance principles. According to him, lenders should also help clients run businesses, but such support was often absent.

Consequences for borrowers and lenders

A committee that studied the situation in the sector found cases in which one person received loans from 23 microfinance institutions. Another borrower had 22 loan accounts at 17 institutions and received a total of 5.217 million Nepalese rupees. At the same time, 81.8% of clients had a loan from only one institution, while 18.2%, or 418,722 people, had loans from two or more.

Borrower groups claim that 42 microfinance institutions continued lending to the same clients in violation of central bank directives. Industry representatives, for their part, say that repayment was affected by campaigns whose participants urged people not to pay their debts.

The problems also affected the lenders themselves: the share of non-performing loans in the sector, which was below 3% until 2022, reached an average of 10.42% by mid-July. At Matribhumi Microfinance, this figure reached a maximum of 26%, according to the central bank.

title: Nepal may miss SAFF Men's Championship for the first time — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal may miss SAFF Men's Championship for the first time — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal will almost certainly not play in the 15th South Asian Football Federation (SAFF) Men's Championship, which Dhaka, Bangladesh, will host in November. The country was given until September 30 to secure the lifting of its FIFA membership suspension, but resolving the situation by the deadline appears unlikely, Kathmandu Post reports.

Deadline for participation

During the group draw on August 1, SAFF gave Nepal two months to resolve the issues. The Nepalese team was not included in any group, but the federation promised to add it to the tournament hosts' group if the FIFA sanction was lifted by September 30.

SAFF General Secretary Purushottam Kattel said the organization would wait for official confirmation from FIFA or the Asian Football Confederation on Nepal's eligibility to participate. According to him, SAFF set this deadline because it expected the situation to be resolved.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Investigation into the football association

FIFA suspended Nepal's membership on June 24 over third-party interference. Amid a conflict between the authorities and the All Nepal Football Association, the Central Investigation Bureau detained ANFA treasurer Rabindra Joshi and finance department employee Sanjeev Pandey on September 18. Investigators also seized computers and laptops from the ANFA complex in Satdobato, Lalitpur.

Bureau chief Uma Prasad Chaturbedi said the probe concerns financial matters, including the purchase and sale of sports kits, the sale of tickets for the 2026 World Cup, and the relocation of Nepal's home match against Bahrain. The bureau said it had not yet coordinated with FIFA and the AFC and that the investigation could continue for a long time.

Nepal Football Players Association president Bikram Lama called the team's possible absence from SAFF a serious blow to Nepalese football. An ANFA representative speaking anonymously blamed the government for the situation and said FIFA would lift the suspension if the association were allowed to operate autonomously.

title: In Nepal, AI tracks in folk style spread on social media — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, AI tracks in folk style spread on social media — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, AI tracks that imitate folk music are increasingly being played on buses and spreading on social media. A columnist for Kathmandu Post believes that such compositions may push performers and the cultural traditions from which they borrow elements into the background.

According to the author, performers of Nepali folk music are often little known to the general public or have a narrow circle of followers. At the same time, traditional songs are preserved thanks to familiar storylines, a dialogic style and ties to local customs. The author suggests that the weak connection between listeners and performers facilitates the spread of generated music.

AI cover and the original song

The column cites “Lamjunge Dadaima Hawa Sarara” as an example. The original composition was released a year earlier by singer and songwriter Jibihang Rai, while the AI cover appeared almost seven months ago. According to the data cited by the author, the AI version has nearly five times more views than the original.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The author also notes that AI tracks are repeatedly used as audio accompaniment on social platforms. The text suggests that the performer of the original song may not have received compensation for the cover’s popularity, although the column contains no information about rights to the composition or payments.

Sound and cultural heritage

In the author’s view, most music-generation models were trained on Western content, so they lack data to reproduce the sound of distinctly South Asian instruments. He describes AI compositions as having a metallic electronic tint and background noise that only imitates traditional instruments.

The column emphasizes that Nepali folk music is connected to local traditions, including songs sung by men and women during courtship. The author mentions panchibaja melodies and the madal rhythm as part of the musical heritage. He also draws attention to youth initiatives to preserve history, traditional crafts and national clothing, including the katharchive.np page and the Bachhittaa brand.

title: In Nepal's flood zone, teachers mourn students who never returned - Yahoo
description: In Nepal's flood zone, teachers mourn students who never returned  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
Each morning at a school in flood-ravaged Nepal, teachers taking attendance are served a painful reminder of the disaster as they mark in red the names of students who never came back.

The catastrophic flood, triggered by a glacial collapse near the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.

Over 5,000 remain missing in the Himalayan nation one month after the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous regions up north.

At the Neelakantha Secondary School in hard-hit Rasuwa district, a teacher marked red circles beside the names of children missing since the August 26 flood.

Unlike more than a dozen schools destroyed by the floods, the Neelakantha school, sitting on relatively higher ground, remained largely intact.

But it lost 70 of its students and four teachers.

"If you look at Rasuwa, you can't find a family that has not lost a family member," principal Madhav Lamichhane told AFP.

"All the students and teachers are going through the same pain."

Most of the missing Neelakantha pupils were on their way to the school from riverside settlements when floodwaters tore through the valley.

"They have lost their lives in this disaster at such a young age. It's a great loss."

"This is the worst situation ever the education sector has experienced," education ministry spokesman Shree Prasad Bhattarai told AFP.

"Returning to learning provides children with a sense of stability, routine and hope at a time when many have experienced significant loss and uncertainty."

For many families, however, sending children back to school was not yet possible.

Some classrooms have been repurposed as relief distribution centres, underscoring the challenges of restoring normalcy.

Teachers say psychological scars may prove even harder to overcome than damaged infrastructure.

title: Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal amid floods - BBC
description: Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal amid floods  BBC
publisher.title: BBC
full_article:
Massive flooding left a government building in western Nepal teetering on the edge of an unstable ledge before it fell into the Daram River.

Witnesses captured the moment that the building in Baglung collapsed on Sunday, 27 September.

Officials removed important documents and computers from the building before it fell, local ward chair Tej Thapa confirmed to the BBC. No one was injured.

Landslides and floods have killed at least 27 people over recent days, according to Nepal's national disaster agency, only weeks after a flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border killed 1,400 people and left thousands more missing.
